ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 3 — Focused Visit (Follow-up) — Elvis Presley — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Three-week review on buprenorphine: withdrawal and cravings, the first benzodiazepine taper step, blood pressure treatment, CPAP, constipation and weight, and planning for a Las Vegas engagement

text.paragraph: Three-week review on buprenorphine, before a Las Vegas engagement. [S]

Mr. Presley returns three weeks after starting buprenorphine. Withdrawal settled on the first day, and he has taken 16 mg every morning since, with mild cravings in the evenings after rehearsals and no other opioid. He had weekly phone contact and two counseling sessions. He has taken diazepam 10 mg four times daily and no alprazolam. He used CPAP on 82% of nights, for an average of 6.1 hours, and is less sleepy in the afternoons (Epworth 9). His home blood pressure has averaged 128/82 on amlodipine with valsartan, without ankle swelling or dizziness. His bowels open every one to two days, so he has stopped the senna. He is anxious about the three-week Las Vegas engagement starting in twelve days. He had to leave for a rehearsal before giving a urine sample. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1974-08-07; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Calm and alert; blood pressure 128/82, pulse 76; weight 108.2 kg

Fatigue, weight gain of about 14 kg in two years, constipation with a bowel movement every five to seven days, loud snoring with daytime sleepiness, and high blood pressure readings, in a man taking two opioids, two benzodiazepines and an appetite suppressant from five prescribers; under evaluation with addiction medicine, a sleep study and home blood pressure readings
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to the documented prescribed drugs and weight gain; superseded when the consultation and tests made the diagnoses.

Obesity, class 1 (BMI 32.5), with prediabetes (hemoglobin A1c 5.8%); recorded without stigma; weight gain began with long touring schedules, night eating after shows and an appetite suppressant that stopped working
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis anchored to his documented weight gain.

Glaucoma secondary to steroids, both eyes, mild stage, after an acute angle-closure episode treated years ago; intraocular pressure controlled on latanoprost under his ophthalmologist; anticholinergic and sympathomimetic drugs to be avoided
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis anchored to his documented glaucoma and the retrospective interpretation of it as steroid-induced; not a claim about his real eyes.

Opioid use disorder, severe, with prescription opioids from more than one prescriber (seven DSM-5-TR criteria, tolerance and withdrawal counted because the opioids were not taken as prescribed); on buprenorphine from the consultation; synthetic modern episode linked to his documented withdrawal from narcotic drugs and prescribed painkillers
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the addiction medicine consultation; person-first language; not a claim about his real diagnosis.

Sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic use disorder (benzodiazepines), moderate (five DSM-5-TR criteria), with two benzodiazepines from two prescribers; combined into diazepam and tapering slowly; synthetic modern episode linked to his documented prescribed sedatives
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the consultation; not a claim about his real diagnosis.
Hypertension, stage 2, confirmed by a home average of 146/94 a week after stopping phentermine; ECG and urine albumin normal
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis confirmed with home readings, anchored to his documented hypertension.
Obstructive sleep apnea, moderate (apnea-hypopnea index 26 an hour, central apnea index 4, oxygen nadir 80% on in-laboratory polysomnography), worsened by opioids and benzodiazepines; on CPAP
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis from a synthetic sleep study.
Opioid-induced constipation (Rome IV), improving after the change to buprenorphine; no alarm features
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis anchored to his documented blockage of the colon; not a claim about megacolon.

Continue 16 mg daily; prescriptions for the engagement sent to one named pharmacy in Las Vegas.

Diazepam 36 mg a day (10 mg three times daily with 2 mg three times daily).
No further step during the engagement.

Hypertension, stage 2 (I10). Home average 128/82; potassium 4.4 and creatinine 1.04 three weeks after starting valsartan. [S]
Continue amlodipine with valsartan.

Obesity, class 1, with prediabetes (E66.811). Weight 108.2 kg. With buprenorphine stable and his bowels regular, tirzepatide can be started; it treats both obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, and its gastrointestinal effects will be watched with his history of constipation. [S]
Tirzepatide 2.5 mg weekly, the first dose today.
Earlier main meal and more walking.
